_about: Screening-level valuation for the ranked companies (Version 2 item 3 + analyst review). Three lenses: listed peers (what the public market pays), deals (what control buyers pay) and a sponsor returns check (the most a buyer could pay and still make its hurdle). Kept separate from the score. Illustrative only, from public data; not a valuation of any company. Skills: valuation-triangulator (lenses and reconciliation), returns-sensitivity (walk-away price, exit flat to entry, debt fixed in pounds).

multiple_ranges._rule: Range applied to latest-year EBITDA. Recurring-type businesses (revenue visibility estimate 0.6 or more) use the services range; project-based businesses use the contractor range. Small EBITDA (under the threshold) takes a size discount.

recurring_services.why: Gamma (UK business communications, 89% recurring revenue) traded near 6x before its bid and was taken private at about 7.6x; Crowe puts listed UK services at 7.5x. Our companies are far smaller, so the range sits at or below these.

project_contractors.why: SPIE, a large listed technical services group, trades near 8x; UK private deals under £250m have a median near 6x. Project-by-project revenue and small size put these at a discount to SPIE.

network_asset_owners.why: Owners of towers and fibre networks are priced by infrastructure funds, well above services firms: VodafoneZiggo's Dutch towers sold at 16.2x 2025 EBITDA (DigitalBridge-led consortium, 2026) and Bite's TeleTower at 16x EBITDAaL (Stonepeak). UK fibre deals are often priced per home and include distressed sales, so the range starts lower.

sponsor_case._rule: Five-year hold, exit at the entry multiple (no multiple expansion), debt sized off EBITDA and held fixed in pounds while the entry price moves, all spare cash repays debt.
sponsor_case._cash: Where a filing has a cash flow statement, capex uses the actual figure and the working-capital drag is 1 minus cash conversion (capped at 30%, never below 0).

listed_infrastructure_funds.name: Cordiant Digital Infrastructure
listed_infrastructure_funds.what: Listed digital infrastructure trust (towers, data centres, fibre)
listed_infrastructure_funds.fact: shares at about a 16% discount to NAV (124p vs 146p, June 2026)
listed_infrastructure_funds.read: Listed buyers of digital infrastructure are themselves priced below their own asset values, so they are unlikely to pay up for small service businesses; trade buyers and mid-market PE are the likelier exits.

market_notes.note: Netomnia, a customer MAP Group has worked for, is being bought by nexfibre (£2bn, Feb 2026), with Virgin Media O2 taking on network construction: check whether MAP keeps that work.

Single MoD PFI contract ending in 2033: the buyer case assumes an exit at the entry multiple after five years, which a contract with two years left would not fetch. Valued on the remaining contract alone (about seven years of free cash flow of roughly £3.9m a year: EBITDA £5.4m less capital spending at 2% of sales and tax at 25%, no extension, no hand-back costs), the business is worth about £19–20m at an 8–10% discount rate, against £32–43m on multiples; after £15.8m of net debt the shares would be worth only about £3–4m.
market_notes.source: Alert Communications accounts FY Mar 2026 (principal activity)

market_notes.note: Owns network assets (towers or fibre). Sellers and infrastructure funds price these well above the 6–8x services range used in this price check, so it is a floor, not a guide to what a seller would accept. The size check uses a 12–18x asset-owner range and any public deal value instead.
